extraction_text: Utathya explains that all beings depend on dharma, and dharma depends on the king.

Utathya describes how sages created the king from the five elements to embody dharma.
Utathya emphasizes that dharma flourishes when the king flourishes, and vice versa.
Utathya states that Brahma created dharma for the welfare of all beings.
Utathya advises the king to abandon desire and anger, and follow dharma as the path to happiness.
Utathya instructs that Brahmins are the source of dharma, and the king should always respect them.
Utathya warns that if Brahmins' desires are not fulfilled, the king faces danger, loses friends, and gains enemies.
Utathya gives the example of Bali, son of Virochana, who became jealous of Brahmins, causing Lakshmi to leave him in anger.
Lakshmi goes to Indra (the slayer of Baka) after leaving Bali.
Sakra (Indra) went to the destroyer of the castle, and Bali felt regret.
Lakshmi (Goddess of Fortune) became angry and left Mandata.
Lakshmi gave birth to a son named Pride with Adharma (Unrighteousness).
Pride repeatedly led gods and asuras to destruction.
King Mandata is advised to avoid Adharma and Pride to maintain his position.
King Mandata is warned about the consequences of neglecting dharma, including social chaos, natural disasters, and omens of destruction.
Uttanka states that timely rain and a king following dharma lead to prosperity and happiness for all beings.
Uttanka explains the duties of the four varnas (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) and the king's role in maintaining order.
Uttanka declares that the king is the creator and destroyer of all beings, and his behavior defines the age (Yuga).
King Mandata's kingdom suffers when he becomes arrogant and neglects dharma (righteous duty).

attributes.relationship: King (Vasumana) seeks guidance from a sage (Vamadeva) on proper rule.

extraction_text: Vamadeva instructs King Vasumana on the principles of righteous kingship.

key_teachings: Follow dharma, as nothing is higher; kings who uphold dharma win the earth.
Use wisdom and dharma as the highest means to success.
A king who uses force and ignores dharma loses both dharma and artha.
Employing evil ministers destroys dharma and leads to the king's downfall.
A king who is arrogant, acts without considering benefit, and follows his whims will be destroyed even if he conquers the earth.
A king who controls his senses, is without envy, and is wise will prosper.
A king should never be self-satisfied regarding dharma, kama (pleasure), artha, wisdom, and friends.
The world functions based on all these. By heeding this advice, a king gains fame, praise, wealth, and subjects.
A king who loves dharma, focuses on dharma and artha, and acts with clear purpose achieves great success.
A king who is not charitable, not merciful, punishes subjects excessively, and is cruel will be quickly destroyed.
A king lacking wisdom, unable to see sinful actions, and of ill repute falls into hell after death.
A king who respects others, is generous, pure in conduct, and discerning is protected by people as they protect themselves.
A king without a teacher, who does not inquire about dharma, amasses wealth, and indulges in pleasures will not prosper long.
A king who consults teachers about dharma, personally attends to worldly affairs, and emphasizes dharma will prosper long.

extraction_text: Vamadeva continues, stating that a strong king who treats the weak unjustly sets a precedent his descendants will follow.

key_teachings: People imitate a wicked king, becoming uncultured, leading to the king's quick ruin.
People depend on the king's proper conduct; even his own people cannot tolerate his improper conduct.
A king who is harsh by nature, disregards scriptures, and acts recklessly will be quickly destroyed.

extraction_text: The text describes the duties and principles of a king (Kshatriya) according to dharma.
A king should not deviate from the ancient ways of victors and vanquished.
A king should not disrespect captured enemies who performed their duties, even if out of hatred.
A king should be capable, pleasant, compassionate in disasters, and will thus win people's affection and not lose prosperity.
If someone is made unhappy, efforts should be made to make them happy again; even unlovable people can become lovable through good deeds.
A king should avoid lying, do good without being asked, and not abandon dharma out of greed, anger, or hatred.
A king should not be embarrassed by inquiries, not boast, not act hastily, not harbor envy, and thus subdue enemies.
A king should not be overly joyful in good times nor overly anxious in bad times, maintain composure in financial difficulties, and remember the welfare of subjects.
A king acting according to his virtues and doing good will succeed and not lose prosperity.
A king should respect loyal, good, and non-betraying virtuous people.
A king should employ those who control senses, are capable, pure in conduct, and loyal.
A king should not employ those who, despite virtues, do not love the king and are envious of the master's wealth.
A king should not employ foolish, sensual, greedy, deceitful, cruel, cunning, ignorant, drunk, gambling, lustful, or hunting-obsessed people, or risk losing prosperity.
A king should first protect himself, then protect those who need protection; if subjects prosper, he will enjoy prosperity.
A king should secretly arrange friends to spy on other kings to avoid harm.
After offending a powerful king, one should not comfort oneself with distance, as he may attack unexpectedly like a vulture.
A noble, well-established king aware of his strength should attack weak enemies, not strong ones.
A king adhering to dharma, acquiring earth through valor, protecting subjects by law, should destroy enemies in battle.
Since everything in the world is destined to perish and insecure, a king should adhere to dharma and protect subjects by law.
Five things make the earth flourish: fortifying defenses, participating in battle, teaching dharma, planning, and ensuring happiness.
A king fulfilling protective duties can enjoy the earth.
A king alone cannot oversee everything; he can delegate to ministers to enjoy the earth long.
People love a king who is generous, shares happiness, mild-tempered, pure in conduct, and does not abandon subjects.
Understanding and adopting the best plan, abandoning one's own ideas, brings stability to the world.
Vamadeva advises King Vasumana on principles of kingship, emphasizing non-violent victory, securing a strong foundation, and righteous conduct.

key_points: A king must have a strong foundation (loyal subjects, satisfied ministers, ample resources) before expansion
Righteous behavior leads to conquest in this life and the next

extraction_text: Bhishma recounts to the listener that King Vasumana followed Vamadeva's advice and urges the listener to do the same to win both worlds.

key_points: Bhishma instructs the listener to follow the same principles for success
